title: H-1B Overhaul Threatens to Shut Indian Students Out of the American Dream
excerpt: A proposed three-year H-1B pause, $200,000 salary floor, and OPT elimination add to the $100,000 fee shock, pushing Indian students toward Canada, the UK, and Germany.
body:
• The End H-1B Visa Abuse Act of 2026 proposes a three-year pause on H-1B issuance, then a permanent cap cut to 25,000 from 85,000
  • A proposed $200,000 minimum salary would disqualify most entry-level roles that Indian graduates typically fill
  • The bill also seeks to eliminate the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, closing the main post-study work pathway
  • These proposals compound the $100,000 H-1B application fee imposed in September 2025, which has already triggered a shift toward alternative destinations

Indian students — who account for more than 70 percent of H-1B visa recipients — face the most severe tightening of America's skilled immigration pathways in decades, as a proposed congressional bill threatens to effectively end the H-1B program as a post-study work route.

The End H-1B Visa Abuse Act of 2026, introduced by Republican Senator Eli Crane, proposes a three-year moratorium on H-1B visa issuance, followed by a permanent reduction of the annual cap from 85,000 to 25,000. The bill also calls for eliminating the Optional Practical Training program, which currently allows international graduates to work in the U.S. for up to three years in STEM fields after completing their degrees.

A $200,000 Barrier

The bill's most immediately disqualifying provision is a proposed minimum salary floor of $200,000 per year for H-1B positions — roughly double to triple the median starting salary for roles that Indian graduates typically enter, including software engineering, data analysis, and management consulting.

"Without OPT, the students will have to leave immediately after their study program because potential recruiter organisations will be wary to pay $100,000 for a fresh graduate over and above their regular compensation."

— Suchindra Kumar, Partner, PwC India

The proposed salary floor would restrict H-1B access almost exclusively to senior hires at large corporations, eliminating the program as a realistic pathway for recent graduates.

Compounding the Fee Shock

These legislative proposals arrive on top of the $100,000 H-1B application fee imposed by the Trump administration in September 2025, which raised costs from roughly $2,000-$5,000 per application. The fee applies to new filings and consular processing, though a clarification from USCIS confirmed that students already in the U.S. who request a change of status are not subject to the charge.

Additional regulatory changes effective later this year include the elimination of "Duration of Status" for F-1 and J-1 visas, replaced by a strict four-year limit, and a reduction of the post-study grace period from 60 to 30 days.

Students Looking Elsewhere

The cumulative impact has accelerated a shift among Indian students toward alternative destinations. Canada offers a three-year post-study work permit, the UK provides a two-to-three-year Graduate Visa, and Germany has expanded English-taught programs with favorable work rights.

"I'll move to Canada or Europe — anywhere that actually wants us."

— Indian student pursuing a master's degree in Texas

Of the roughly 400,000 Indian students who go abroad annually for higher education, the U.S. has been the dominant destination. But consultants report that inquiry volumes for American universities have declined while interest in Canada, the UK, Australia, and Germany has surged.

Business groups and industry coalitions have filed legal challenges arguing that the executive branch lacked authority to impose the $100,000 fee. Courts may issue injunctions that alter implementation, but for now, the regulatory uncertainty itself is deterring both students and the employers who would sponsor them.
nri_angle: Indian students and their families face direct disruption as the primary post-study work pathway in America narrows dramatically.
author: Diaspora Desk
